Our research investigates how users of Signal, a popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app, perceive and utilize the PIN security feature. Through a study involving 10 Signal users, we discovered that most participants either didn't understand the purpose of the PIN or didn't know how to set it up. Those who did use the PIN often employed weak passwords, unaware of its security benefits. Notably, users who set up a PIN tended to use it for protecting sensitive messages, whereas users who didn't use it perceived it as unnecessary. To address these issues, we suggest implementing in-app prompts to educate users on the purpose of the PIN and how to set it up, as well as incorporating a visual indicator of the PIN's strength.

The growing use of solar power in energy grids poses a significant challenge 
due to its intermittent nature. To address this issue, researchers have been 
developing methods to optimize the integration of solar power into energy grids. 
In this paper, a novel approach is proposed, which involves a specific type of 
Gaussian quadrature that prioritizes solar power measurements taken during the 
daytime. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to any solar power 
data set, whereas existing methods are limited to specific types of data. The 
efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated through numerical experiments 
using both synthetic and real-world data.

The curvature of the loss landscape in deep neural networks significantly impacts their training, and the Hessian matrix is commonly used to capture this curvature. However, Hessian-based optimization methods are often impractical due to their high computational costs. An alternative approach involves approximating the Hessian using the generalized Gauss-Newton matrix, which is more manageable. Despite this improvement, the Hessian approximation still suffers from high dimensionality. To address this issue, we introduce a new low-rank approximation technique that effectively reduces the Hessian approximation's dimensionality. Our proposed method involves a two-step process: first, we apply a low-rank approximation to the Hessian approximation, and then we use a novel technique to further compress the Hessian approximation. The result is a low-rank Hessian approximation that can be efficiently computed and updated during the training process. The proposed method is evaluated on a variety of deep neural network architectures and loss landscape curvature estimation tasks, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing the curvature of the loss landscape.

Numerous languages categorize nouns into distinct classes, assigning each class a unique grammatical gender.  In languages where gendered inflections are common, such as Spanish, gender influences word usage, affecting verb conjugation and article selection.  To explore how gendering affects the representation of words, we examined German, a language with highly regular grammatical gendering.  By analyzing a German corpus, we discovered that gendered inflections contribute to gender accuracy rates of 80% to 90%, making them a valuable indicator of word class.  In contrast, German's lack of gendered inflections results in lower accuracy rates of 60% to 70%.  Furthermore, we found that gendered inflections provide a more consistent and interpretable representation of words, reducing variability in word representations by 10% to 20%.  In addition, we discovered that gendered inflections capture semantic information, such as animacy, and that this effect is more pronounced in languages with more regular gendering systems.  Overall, our findings suggest that gendered inflections play a crucial role in shaping the representation of words in languages with regular gendering systems.

We've demonstrated that the charmability index of an arithmetic group has a lower bound in terms of its L^2-stiffness exponent, which in turn is limited from above by the sum of the weights of its fundamental representations. This result is applied to show that the stiffness exponent of GL_n(Z) is at most n^2(1 + 1/6n).

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of object placement estimation for unseen categories by leveraging pre-trained object detectors and visual features. We leverage the capabilities of a pre-trained detector to achieve pose estimation for new object categories without requiring any modifications to the network or training data. We introduce a novel, differentiable optimization framework that achieves pose estimation by minimizing the reprojection error between 2D and 3D keypoints. This framework is compatible with both 2D and 3D object detection outputs, allowing us to utilize 2D detection results to obtain initial pose estimates, which are then refined through optimization. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach on a benchmark dataset and achieve state-of-the-performace results for 2D detection-based initialization.

Traffic forecasting is a crucial task for intelligent transportation systems, and sparse traffic data is a common challenge. Existing methods struggle to effectively handle this issue, and we propose a novel approach called SAEL. This approach leverages the similarity between time steps to extract relevant attributes from sparse traffic data, and we demonstrate its efficacy through extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

This paper presents VACA, a novel class of variational graph autoencoders designed to simulate complex interventions and alternative scenarios on intricate networks. By leveraging advanced probabilistic inference techniques, including mean field variational inference, VACA enables efficient computation of otherwise intractable likelihoods. As a result, VACA can accurately model intricate dependencies between latent variables, outperforming existing methods that rely on simplified assumptions. Furthermore, VACA's ability to accurately model these dependencies is demonstrated through its application to a simulated binary network, where it achieves higher likelihoods compared to baseline models.

We present initial results from the REAL-time Acquisition (REALTA) system, a cutting-edge technology that enables the LOFAR station to rapidly respond to alerts about transient sky phenomena. This system was integrated into the station's data processing pipeline, allowing for real-time imaging and image reconstruction. In a recent trial, REALTA successfully identified and localized two alerts originating from the ATCAE project, providing precise imaging of the phenomena at the time of the alerts. This achievement demonstrates the feasibility of REALTA in guiding rapid follow-up observations of transient events, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of these phenomena.

The synergy between metaphotonics and machine learning holds the potential to revolutionize the development of future photonic systems. By integrating machine learning with metamaterials and metaphotonics, researchers can now design and optimize these devices with unprecedented efficiency. This work explores the intersection of these two fields, offering a comprehensive review of the fundamental principles of metamaterials and metaphotonics, as well as the principles of machine learning. Furthermore, the review delves into the applications of metaphotonics and machine learning in various fields, such as optical communications, sensing, and computing, and discusses the challenges and future directions of this interdisciplinary research.

This study investigates how pre-release attributes influence a film's potential revenue,
revealing that attributes such as genre, director, and cast can significantly
affect a movie's success, even before it is released. By analyzing a dataset of
2,000+ movies from 2011-2019, we found that certain attributes are more predictive
of a film's revenue than others, and that these relationships vary depending on the
genre of the movie. Our results have important implications for the film industry,
as they suggest that pre-release attributes can be used to make more informed
decisions about which movies to invest in and how to market them.

This study examines the intricate interplay between frequency and voltage stability in a power grid, focusing on the simultaneous operation of primary frequency control and the dynamic behavior of inverters. The analysis reveals that the interconnection of the grid's frequency and voltage control systems can lead to the emergence of new stable voltage dynamics, characterized by a specific oscillation frequency. The study's findings are validated through the use of a specific inverter model, the generalized impedance model, and the development of a simplified two-node system that captures the dual-frequency dynamics. The research also explores the implications of this interaction on the grid's stability, showing that the presence of fast-acting inverters can introduce new stability risks, even in grids that were previously considered stable. The study's outcomes have significant implications for the design and operation of future power systems, highlighting the need for careful consideration of the interplay between frequency and voltage control dynamics.

Cyber-physical systems have revolutionized various sectors, including transportation, healthcare, and manufacturing, by enabling automation and remote control. As cyber-physical systems become increasingly interconnected, they form vast networks of systems that require efficient management and coordination. This research focuses on enhancing these networks by integrating intelligent agents that can adapt and optimize performance. Agent-based optimization is proposed as a solution to tackle the scalability and complexity challenges associated with managing cyber-physical networks. This approach enables the development of scalable and efficient solutions, as demonstrated by a case study in a smart grid system.

Blazars, a subset of active galactic nuclei, display a distinctive pattern in their optical to gamma-ray spectra, with two prominent humps.  The origin of this double-humped emission pattern remains a subject of debate, with some models suggesting a single-peak process and others a two-peak inverse Compton scattering mechanism.  To address this issue, we developed a model-independent approach to analyze blazar spectra, utilizing a Monte-Carlo method to determine the degree of polarization in their emission.  By applying this approach to 11 blazars, we found that their spectra exhibit significant polarization, with the highest levels observed in the ultraviolet/soft X-ray band.  These findings support the double-humped emission model and provide new insights into the physical processes driving blazar emission.

Analytic continuation is a mathematical concept that can be applied to complex systems, such as those with intricate structures, to uncover hidden patterns and relationships. This paper explores the potential of analytic continuation in the field of cosmology, where it can be used to uncover a simplified and more coherent picture of the universe's structure. The authors argue that the apparent contradictions and inconsistencies in the standard cosmological model may be a result of the limited scope of current theories, and that a more comprehensive understanding of the universe's structure can be achieved through a more nuanced application of analytic continuation. The paper also discusses the potential of this approach in the context of the Hubble tension, where it can be used to uncover a more accurate measurement of the universe's expansion rate. The authors conclude that the potential of analytic continuation in the field of cosmology is still largely untapped, and that further research in this area may lead to significant breakthroughs in our understanding of the universe's structure.

We've developed a quantum hypothesis testing framework for identifying pure states with given symmetry properties. This framework is rooted in quantum information and operator algebra, allowing us to derive a method for distinguishing between the null and alternative states based on their representation of symmetry. This approach is applicable to various scenarios, including detecting bosonic Gaussian states and rotationally invariant states. Notably, our method yields an optimal strategy for detecting thermal states, outperforming conventional approaches.

Baryon creation through a specific quantized process is investigated, where a QCD flux tube with helical properties breaks down into smaller components, forming mesons and baryons. Baryon formation occurs when a fragment, specifically a fundamental representation, detaches from the string and interacts with a quark, while the remaining part becomes a gauge-invariant excitation. Baryon momentum is determined by the frequencies of quark oscillations within the fragment, constrained by the energy available. Baryon properties, such as momentum, are calculated and compared with Baryon momentum obtained from string fragmentation models. Baryon momentum obtained from this model is consistent with Baryon momentum obtained from string fragmentation models.

The travel-time measurements of north-south sound waves around active regions are influenced by currents within those regions. To understand this effect, we used data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory to create three-dimensional models of active regions and their surrounding areas, incorporating the horizontal flow of plasma. We then simulated sound waves traveling through these models and calculated the time it takes for these waves to reach specific points. We found that currents within active regions cause significant delays in the travel time of sound waves, with a notable difference between north and south paths. This difference is primarily due to the flow of plasma from the center of the region to its periphery, with northward paths experiencing a delay and southward paths experiencing an acceleration. We also discovered that the flow of plasma from the center of the region to its periphery is not uniform, with some areas experiencing a significant delay and others experiencing an acceleration. These findings have significant implications for understanding the behavior of active regions and their impact on the sun's atmosphere.

Primordial magnetic fields may have been created during the universe's inflation period and could have a significant impact on cosmic structure formation. However, the origin of these fields remains uncertain. A new study found that primordial magnetic fields can generate gravitational waves within specific frequency ranges, including the one detected by Pulsar Timing Arrays. The research indicates that the energy density of these magnetic fields can create a detectable gravitational wave signal, with characteristics that can be distinguished from other sources. The analysis shows that the presence of these magnetic fields can be identified through the spectral shape and anisotropic sky distribution of the gravitational wave signal. The research also highlights the potential for future projects like the Square Kilometre Array to significantly enhance the detection capabilities of Pulsar Timing Arrays.

Light field technology has garnered significant attention due to its capacity to provide an immersive 3D visual experience and capture detailed depth information. However, the substantial data requirements for light field images pose a significant challenge. To address this issue, researchers have developed various compression techniques, with the latest advancements leveraging deep learning to achieve superior compression ratios. A novel compression method has been proposed, utilizing a predictive model to identify and eliminate redundancies in light field data. This method employs a pre-determined parallax map to generate a mapping between light field layers, thereby reducing data storage requirements. A novel loss function has been designed to optimize image quality and compression efficiency, with the method's effectiveness demonstrated through a comparison with state-of-the-art compressors, showcasing improved performance in terms of compression ratio and visual quality.

In cross-lingual information retrieval, a multilingual embedding model maps queries and documents into a shared semantic space, enabling retrieval across languages. However, recent advancements in large language models have led to the development of non-autonomous retrieval models that consider the context of neighboring terms. This study investigates the potential synergy between interactive and non-autonomous models for cross-lingual retrieval and presents the first application of non-autonomous models in this area. We present two novel approaches that leverage the strengths of both model types: a hybrid approach that uses the output of an interactive model to enhance a non-autonomous one, and a multi-task learning framework that trains a single model to perform the tasks of an interactive and a non-autonomous model simultaneously. Experimental results demonstrate that these approaches outperform standalone interactive and non-autonomous models, with a 15.4% improvement over the best baseline.

This study compares various small-area estimation methods using data from the 2016 Demographic and Health Survey in Malawi, a country with limited resources. A total of 1,200 hypothetical areas were created, and different estimation methods were applied to both complete and imputed datasets. The survey data was pre-processed to address missing values and non-response bias. The results indicate that the weighted least squares method of calibration outperformed other methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, and that using imputed datasets can significantly improve estimation accuracy. The study recommends that health and policy decision-makers working with survey data in low- and middle-income countries should consider using the weighted least squares method of calibration and that data pre-processing is essential to obtain reliable estimates.

The concept of quantum wagering has been explored in the context of discrete systems, specifically qubits, and it has been demonstrated that this approach can consistently outperform classical methods. Building upon this concept, quantum wagering is now being considered in the context of continuous variable systems, and a new method has been proposed that utilizes coherent states and Gaussian strategies. The results indicate that, in the context of the Wagner game, this approach can consistently outperform both classical methods and qubit-based strategies.

Theoretical investigations into the electronic properties of two-dimensional materials consisting of four atoms per layer, specifically MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds, have been conducted using density functional theory. Our findings indicate that these materials exhibit a unique stacking-independent exciton, characterized by a substantial energy gap between the valence band maximum and conduction band minimum. Additionally, we discovered that the electronic band structure of these materials is influenced by the arrangement of atomic layers, with specific stacking configurations leading to distinct quasiparticle energy gaps.

The LHCb experiment has conducted a search for the decay of a sum sign particle into a proton and a muon pair, and the results show that this process occurs at a rate significantly higher than predicted by the standard model of particle physics. A statistical analysis of data collected in 2011 and 2012 from proton-proton collisions at a center of mass energy of 7 and 8 TeV respectively revealed an excess of events, amounting to 6.1 standard deviations above background noise. This anomaly suggests the presence of new physics beyond the standard model, and the probability of this occurrence is estimated at 1.2 times 10 to the power of -9.

The process of star formation, which involves the creation of protoplanetary disks, is still not fully understood. To address this knowledge gap, researchers have conducted a study on the evolution of a star-forming region, focusing on the transition from a stationary core to a disk system. By analyzing the chemical and physical properties of the core over time, the study found that the core's breakdown led to the formation of a disk, which in turn facilitated the formation of a star and its surrounding disk system. The study's findings suggest that the core's initial conditions play a crucial role in determining the outcome of star formation, and that the process of disk formation is likely to be a common occurrence in star-forming regions.

Astronomical observations through the atmosphere are distorted due to the differing refractive indices of air at various wavelengths. To counteract this effect, astronomers use Atmospheric Dispersion Uniter (ADU) devices. The effectiveness of these devices relies on an accurate understanding of the atmospheric refractive index as a function of wavelength. This paper outlines the development of a new model for the refractive index, which is based on a comprehensive analysis of existing atmospheric data. The results of this analysis are presented and compared to current models used in the literature.

In this study, we present a Bayesian sparsity-inducing model for multi-period time series analysis, where the goal is to identify the most relevant features in high-dimensional data across multiple periods. Our model integrates the Dirichlet process prior with the standard linear regression model, allowing for the creation of distinct, sparse models for each time period. By leveraging the conjugate properties of Bayesian inference, we develop an efficient variational inference algorithm to approximate the complex posterior distribution in high-dimensional settings. Our approach is demonstrated to be highly effective on both simulated and real-world datasets, where it outperforms existing methods in terms of computational speed and predictive accuracy.

This note establishes a correspondence between Pontryagin duality and constant logic, revealing a connection to a well-known duality in uniform spaces. We also outline a plan to generalize this correspondence to other types of groups, including those that are not compactly generated.

Federated learning, a privacy-preserving machine learning technique, has been extensively researched in recent years. However, the current literature on this topic has primarily focused on its privacy aspects, neglecting the challenges of addressing fairness issues. This paper aims to bridge this gap by investigating the implications of differential privacy and statistical parity in the context of federated learning. We demonstrate that a simple approach of adjusting local model parameters can effectively achieve fairness while maintaining the accuracy of global models. Furthermore, we propose a novel method for adjusting these parameters that surpasses the limitations of existing methods, such as those proposed by Chierichetti et al. and Hardt et al. Our approach is validated through experiments on various datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in addressing fairness issues in FL.

In this research, a supersymmetric minimal extension of a $U(1)_X$ model is proposed, incorporating a right-handed Majorana neutrino field, $\chi$, to explain dark energy. The model's gauge symmetry is derived from a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge group, which undergoes spontaneous symmetry breaking at a high energy scale. This results in the $Z_2$ discrete symmetry breaking, which in turn breaks the fermion number symmetry and generates a mass for the $\chi$ field. The $U(1)_X$ gauge boson, $Z'$, acquires a mass of approximately 1-10 TeV, and its decay width is primarily determined by the decay of $Z' \rightarrow \chi \bar{\chi}$. The model's parameters are constrained by LHC searches for heavy neutral leptons and $Z'$ searches, as well as constraints from beam dump experiments and neutrino oscillation data. The $Z'$ mass is found to be in the range of 3-10 TeV, and its decay branching ratio into $\chi \bar{\chi}$ is primarily responsible for the dark energy phenomenon.

In a wireless network powered by the sky, a new method has been developed to boost its performance by harnessing the potential of a smart, reconfigurable surface. This innovative technique aims to mitigate the negative effects of unwanted signal interference on wireless power transfer and data transmission. To achieve this goal, a cost-effective approach is presented that leverages the surface's phase shift capabilities to optimize the transfer of energy and information, thereby maximizing the network's overall throughput. The optimization process is further simplified by employing a deep learning model that bypasses the need for real-time channel information, thus reducing the computational burden. The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated through numerical simulations, showcasing its ability to significantly enhance the network's throughput.

The study of neutron-rich $^{186}$Hg, with 100 neutrons, is of significant interest as it marks the onset of the N=100 shell gap in the region beyond the doubly magic $^{184}$Hg. A comprehensive investigation of the $\beta$-decay properties of $^{186}$Hg has been conducted using the TRIUMF ISOLDE facility, employing $\beta$-$\gamma$ coincidence and Doppler-shift correlation techniques. The results show that the $\beta$-decay of $^{186}$Hg is characterized by a 6.0(2) second half-life, along with 10 identified $\gamma$ transitions spanning 400 to 1200 keV. A total of 11 levels have been identified, with 8 of them linked to the ground state. A four-level sub-ground state cascade has been discovered, along with a 5/2+ ground state. A comprehensive level scheme has been developed, along with spin and parity assignments for the observed states. A $\beta$-decay strength distribution analysis reveals that the observed strength is in accordance with theoretical predictions. We explore a unified framework where right-handed neutrinos serve as both dark matter and facilitate the generation of matter in the universe through the seesaw mechanism. The interaction between dark matter and the right-handed neutrinos is found to be a crucial factor in the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. We analyze the conditions under which dark matter and right-handed neutrinos coexist, and we examine how this interplay impacts the universe's matter asymmetry. Our study reveals that dark matter's presence can either enhance or suppress the universe's matter asymmetry, depending on the nature of the dark photon.

This study presents a novel, data-driven control approach that enables control systems to be learned from limited data and multiple tasks simultaneously. The proposed method, known as L3DS, stands for Learning to Learn from Scarcely Data and Side Information. L3DS utilizes a single, transferable policy that can be applied to various tasks, with side information used to distinguish between them. The approach is demonstrated using a complex humanoid robot system, which successfully learns to perform multiple tasks, such as reaching, walking, swimming, and flying, using data from only 10 trials. The results show that L3DS outperforms existing methods, with significantly reduced sample complexity, and allows for efficient adaptation to new tasks, such as reaching from different initial states, with minimal data requirements.

We establish a novel set of Ward identities in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, which governs the correlation functions of degenerate degenerate fields resulting from the fusion of two primary fields. These identities provide an alternative framework for understanding the degenerate correlators, which can be solved using the Belavin-Polyakov-Zamolodchikov equations. Furthermore, our results confirm the validity of specific BPZ solutions, which had been proposed by D. Chicherin and A. Gerasimov.

Unsupervised image generation has seen significant advancements with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), particularly in producing high-quality images. However, GANs face a persistent challenge in generating realistic images that align with the data distribution, often resulting in mode collapse. To address this limitation, researchers have explored the application of supervised learning techniques to enhance GAN performance. This paper introduces a novel approach, the Relation GAN, which incorporates triplet loss to guide the generator in producing more authentic images. By leveraging the discriminator to distinguish between real and fake data, the framework enables the generation of high-quality, supervised images. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the framework in producing realistic images on a variety of datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, LSUN Church, and CelebA.

We have developed an enhanced version of the Twin-Field Quantum Key Distribution protocol, referred to as TFKD, which overcomes the need for phase locking. In TFKD, the source of entangled photons is positioned at the legitimate user's end, allowing the other user to select the measurement basis. By employing this setup, the protocol achieves higher key rates and improved key distances compared to its previous iteration. Furthermore, the TFKD protocol shares many characteristics with the BB84 protocol, including the use of pre-shared basis information and the absence of phase synchronization requirements.

This paper investigates the Toeplitz algebra of a Fejér kernel, a kernel related to the Szegő kernel, and demonstrates its unitary equivalence to the Cuntz algebra. Furthermore, we explore the structure of Toeplitz algebras generated by the Riesz and Bloch kernels. We also establish the structure of Toeplitz algebras on the Riesz space and prove that the Toeplitz operator associated with the function z(1-z) on the Riesz space is not a Fredholm operator. We also identify conditions for when Toeplitz operators with the symbol z^k are Fredholm and calculate their indices. We also explore the structure of Toeplitz algebras on the Riesz space and establish a relationship between them and the Hardy space. We also explore the structure of Toeplitz algebras on the Hardy space and establish a relationship between them and the Riesz space.

Recent advancements in object identification have been driven by the concept of open vocabulary object identification, which enables the detection of unfamiliar objects. A key challenge in this area is the lack of precise annotations in existing datasets. To address this limitation, we propose a new approach that uses bounding-box labels derived from dense description data. This approach is based on a two-stage process that combines visual and textual information to achieve accurate detection. To our knowledge, this is the first method to achieve object identification using bounding-box labels for open vocabulary tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets, including COCO-PEDES and Visual Genome.

The Rho Ophiuchus molecular cloud complex, a well-studied area of star formation, is home to the S1 ionization front, which marks the boundary between ionized and neutral gas. Our research, utilizing data from the Herschel Space Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and the Spitzer Space Telescope, provides the most detailed examination of the S1 region to date. Our findings reveal that the S1 ionization front is part of a larger, complex structure that includes a 10-degree arc of ionized gas, which is the result of the interaction between the gas and a nearby star. This structure is accompanied by a dense layer of atomic hydrogen, which is the result of the gas's interaction with the surrounding medium. Our research also shows that the gas is the result of the interaction between the gas and a nearby star, which is the result of the gas's interaction with the surrounding medium.

Transformer-based models have significantly advanced natural language processing,
particularly in text classification tasks, where veracity assessment is crucial.
Veracity refers to the accuracy and reliability of a text's content, and accurate
assessment is essential for combating misinformation and fake news. This survey
reviews the latest developments in veracity assessment using Transformer models,
starting with a definition of veracity and its underlying principles. It then
discusses the creation of Transformer-based text representations and their
utilization in veracity prediction, highlighting the benefits and limitations of
existing approaches. Furthermore, the paper explores the impact of veracity
assessment on downstream tasks, such as opinion extraction and sentiment
analysis, and outlines future research directions and challenges in this field.

This study compares two factor models, one with time-invariant factor loadings and another with time-varying factor loadings, to forecast mortality rates. We find that the time-invariant factor model outperforms the time-varying factor model in terms of accuracy. We also use the time-invariant factor model to project future mortality rates and investigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on these projections.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a powerful tool for automatically designing neural network architectures, yet it is computationally expensive, often requiring hundreds of thousands of training iterations. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed various transfer-based NAS methods to reuse previously evaluated architectures, but these approaches frequently suffer from interference issues, where the selection of subsequent search spaces is influenced by past evaluations rather than their actual performance. This paper investigates the phenomenon of interference in NAS and proposes a novel method to alleviate it, allowing for more effective and transfer-based architecture searches.

This paper presents an overview of univariate and multivariate time series analysis techniques, specifically focusing on the time series feature extraction process. We outline methodologies for computing essential features, including mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, and others, which are crucial for characterizing time series data. We then introduce the theft package, an R library that facilitates automated theft detection and time series analysis, and demonstrate its capabilities through a series of illustrative examples.

We introduce the concept of radial convergence and radial convergence speed, which enables us to establish a clear criterion for a CAT(0) space to be geodesically complete. This criterion is based on the property that every half-line in such a space is either a radial convergent curve or a radially fast curve.

Assessing the quality of machine translation output is a crucial aspect of evaluating its performance. This study employs a Bayesian approach to evaluate the reliability of human assessors in reviewing machine translation. The analysis involves using a dataset of 100 pairs of translated texts, which were evaluated by ten human translators. The research investigates the influence of various factors on translator reliability, including the source and target languages, translated texts, and translator expertise. The results reveal that experienced translators generally demonstrate higher reliability, whereas source and target languages, as well as translated texts, have a negligible impact on reliability. The findings also indicate that the Bayesian model effectively accounts for the variability in translated texts, thereby providing a more accurate assessment of translator reliability.

The unitary S-matrix framework is used to analyze and understand quantum transport in complex open systems. In this context, eigenchannels provide a natural basis for describing scattering processes. Researchers have previously applied the principles of orthogonality and completeness to derive exact sum rules for these eigenchannels. In this study, a novel approach is developed to derive exact sum rules for the energy-dependent contributions of eigenchannels. The method relies on a modified version of the completeness principle, which is derived by considering a set of complete, energy-dependent states. The approach is demonstrated through two examples: one involving a conservative system and another a dissipative system, both with time-reversal symmetry.

In the realm of machine learning, pruning techniques have been gaining traction as a means to enhance model efficiency and reduce computational costs. A novel pruning method called the sensitivity-based pruning (SBP) algorithm has been developed, which outperforms traditional pruning methods by leveraging the sensitivity of weights to the overall model's performance. By iteratively pruning the least impactful weights, SBP can create highly efficient sparse models. Our research explores the application of SBP to two types of neural network architectures, namely convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and fully connected neural networks (FCNNs), to determine whether CNNs are inherently superior to FCNNs in terms of pruning capabilities. By comparing the pruning results of SBP on both architectures, we aim to shed light on the effectiveness of CNNs and the potential of other network designs.

In the context of a lottery, an individual holds a ticket, which is a subset of numbers from a larger pool, and the goal is to maximize the expected profit. The expected profit is a function of the expected value of the winning prize, and the cost of the ticket. The expected value of the winning prize is a function of the expected number of people who win the lottery, and the expected number of people who win the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who buy the lottery is a function of the expected number of people who buy the lottery, and the expected number of people who

The critical behavior of a system that is invariant under O(N) symmetry and has a 4-component field is described by a mathematical model. This behavior is influenced by a parameter, denoted as epsilon, which measures the deviation from three dimensions. A key parameter in this system is the anomalous exponent of its first component, denoted as eta1. A study has calculated a specific term in this exponent to a high degree of precision, specifically at a certain power of epsilon, by using a complex series expansion. This study has calculated ten terms in this series, which is a significant achievement. This study has also found that the calculated values of this series, when extrapolated, are in good agreement with previous calculations using a different method.

Valley Hall currents are generated by applying a magnetic field to materials with two-dimensional properties, resulting in currents that flow in opposite directions in valleys with opposite signs. However, research has shown that this effect can be amplified without a magnetic field in certain materials, like graphene and transition metal dichalcogenides, due to interactions between electrons and phonons. Our research reveals that even when these materials are not doped, these interactions can still produce significant valley Hall currents, comparable to those generated by magnetic fields. The strength of these currents depends on the phonon mode involved and can be influenced by temperature, reaching maximum values at specific temperatures. Our findings demonstrate that novel electron-phonon coupling mechanisms can significantly enhance valley Hall conductivity, opening up new possibilities for developing novel devices.

We successfully submitted a solution to the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation challenge, which involved adapting models from source datasets to unseen target datasets without direct access to the latter. Our approach combined several techniques, including self-supervised learning, data augmentation, and ensemble methods, to achieve high performance across various subchallenges. Specifically, we utilized self-supervised learning with self-supervised contrastive learning, and then fine-tuned the model on the target dataset using a combination of source and target data. Additionally, we employed ensemble methods to improve the model's robustness and generalization. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques in addressing the subchallenges, and provide insights into potential future directions for research in this area.

A widely used dimensionality reduction method, t-SNE, has been effective in visualizing high-dimensional data, but it's not suitable for use in downstream tasks due to its lack of preservation of global data structure. To address this limitation, we developed a representation learning framework that combines the benefits of t-SNE with the properties of spectral methods. By integrating t-SNE into a loss function, we can leverage its local structure preservation while leveraging the global structure preservation of spectral methods. To further improve the learning process, we proposed a novel, differentiable approximation of the t-SNE negative log-likelihood, called $\phi$-SNE, which can be used in conjunction with stochastic gradient descent. To address the limitations of traditional t-SNE, we also introduced a novel variant, $\phi$-VF-SNE, which is designed to work with data that resides on the surface of a unit sphere. Our approach was evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and we demonstrated its superiority over existing methods in terms of its ability to preserve the global structure of the data.

The diagrammatic Monte Carlo method is used to investigate the properties of a Fermi polaron within a two-dimensional fermionic sea. By employing a novel approach that uses continuous-time diagrams, the proposed algorithm allows for the efficient calculation of the polaron's self-energy. The results obtained from this method show that the two-particle binding energy of a fermion-fermion pair is in good agreement with previous numerical findings, while the diagrammatic approach provides insights into the interaction between the particles. Furthermore, the diagrammatic method reveals that the nature of the polaron's excitation spectrum is dependent on the strength of the inter-particle interaction, transitioning from a fermionic to a bosonic character as the interaction becomes stronger.

We've developed a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing strategy to model complex fermionic systems, leveraging a native fermionic interaction Hamiltonian and supplementing it with digital corrections to achieve desired simulations. By employing this approach, we can overcome some limitations of purely digital simulation methods, which often require extensive gate sequences. Our experiments demonstrate that a significant reduction in the number of digital gates can be achieved, specifically in the fermionic Hubbard model, where we've found that a considerable decrease in the number of digital gates can be attained by using a hybrid approach, resulting in more accurate simulations.

We introduce a family of graphs, known as generalized Petersen graphs, denoted by GP(n,k), for which we derive a straightforward method to count the number of specific graph configurations, such as independent vertex sets, graph colorings, and matchings. This yields recursive formulas for associated polynomial sequences. Our analysis reveals that these polynomial sequences exhibit unimodality and log-concavity under certain conditions.

We've discovered a connection between the Veekh curve's genus 6 surface self-maps, known as the Hitchin connection, and a curve's genus 4 surface self-maps. This relationship allows us to express the Lyapunov exponents of the former in terms of those of the latter, thereby providing a straightforward calculation for the former.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant disruptions to the global economy, prompting governments to implement measures such as lockdowns and social distancing. These actions have led to a shift in work practices, with many organizations adopting remote work arrangements. This study investigates the impact of remote work on the effectiveness of Scrum projects, with a focus on Scrum ceremonies and team performance. Through a combination of surveys and interviews, we analyzed the experiences of Scrum teams working from home and found that certain factors, such as communication challenges and changes in team dynamics, can influence project success. Our findings suggest that organizations should consider the unique needs of remote Scrum teams and adapt their processes accordingly to mitigate potential risks and improve project outcomes.

The Gau-Wu Value, a parameter in matrices with nonnegative off-diagonal entries, is defined as the minimum eigenvalue of the matrix with the off-diagonal entries negated. This parameter has been studied extensively, with a specific focus on its properties in irreducible matrices. This research provides a precise formula for the Gau-Wu Value in matrices of size 4 and generalizes this formula for irreducible matrices. Additionally, a specific formula is given for the Gau-Wu Value in arrowhead matrices, and it is shown that the Gau-Wu Value of a specific arrowhead matrix matches the minimum eigenvalue of a modified matrix with the same size.

In heavy-ion collisions, the elliptical shape of the initial nuclei influences the movement of charged particles, providing insight into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma. Researchers have been studying the flow of electrons generated from the decay of charm quarks to understand the interaction between electrons and the QGP. The electrons' momentum is affected by both the number of collisions they undergo and the density of the QGP, making them a suitable probe for studying the QGP's properties. The ALICE collaboration has been investigating the elliptical flow of electrons in Pb-Pb collisions at a specific energy level, with a focus on understanding the influence of charm-quark fragmentation on the elliptical flow measurements. The results of this study will be presented at the 58th International Conference on High Energy Physics.

We've developed a new statistical model for time series data, called the Chromatic Alpha Model, which is an extension of the traditional Alphas model. This model is more flexible and can capture a broader range of dynamics in complex systems. Our model is based on a combination of a hidden Markov model and a time-varying point process, where the transition between states is determined by the Alphas model. By incorporating the concept of persistence, we can extract meaningful information about the underlying structure of the data. Our results show that the chromatic Alpha model can effectively capture the dynamics of real-world systems, such as the stock market and weather patterns. We have also demonstrated that the model can be used for prediction and inference tasks, and that it outperforms other baseline models in terms of accuracy and interpretability.

In a K-user interference network, we investigate the advantage of optimal power control over binary power control in terms of GDoF, and find that this benefit is at least a factor of the square root of K. This is achieved by first establishing a lower bound on the GDoF gain of optimal power control over a specific binary power control scheme, and then demonstrating that this scheme is GDoF optimal in a specific interconnection pattern. This result is further supported by a general analysis showing that, in a specific interconnection pattern, binary and optimal power control schemes are GDoF equivalent.

Formal concept analysis has been widely applied in data mining and knowledge discovery, particularly in categorizing data. However, its traditional approach is limited to rigid frameworks, making it unsuitable for dynamic environments where new data can be unreliable or unexpected. To address this, we've developed an adaptable categorization framework grounded in fuzzy formal concept analysis and the Dempster-Shafer evidence model. This framework enables the evaluation of categorization results in uncertain contexts and can handle unforeseen data. We've also devised an efficient method for incrementally updating the framework when new information becomes available. Our approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through a practical case study in an auditing context.

We introduce a novel Poisson process, the stitching process, which generates random patterns by merging two other Poisson processes, one defining the locations and the other the sizes of intervals. We demonstrate that this construction can be reimagined through the lens of marked point processes, offering a clearer understanding of its properties. We explore the statistical characteristics of the stitching process, focusing on its run-length distribution and providing a concrete example of its application in modeling the random placement of sensors.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle incorporates quantum gravity effects into the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, leading to a modified transformation that affects the coordinates of space and time. This modification has significant implications for both the Lorentz and Galilean transformations, which underpin special and classical relativity respectively. By applying the GUP-modified transformation, we derive a new relationship between the coordinates of space and time, which is dependent on the quantum gravity length scale. This new relationship has profound consequences for our understanding of the relationship between the coordinates of space and time, and may have significant implications for our understanding of the universe.

We investigate a data center allocation issue where a data center manager must distribute a finite number of processing units among multiple clients, each with distinct tasks. The processing units can be utilized by a single client at a time or be shared by multiple clients. The shared usage of these units results in performance degradation, which is influenced by the number of clients utilizing a single unit. The processing speed of each client on a single unit is represented by their individual capacity, and the speed of data transfer between tasks is represented by their edge weights. The processing units are allocated to minimize the total time it takes to complete all tasks, which is an NP-hard problem. The problem is reformulated as an integer programming problem, and a new algorithm is developed to solve it, which is then used to obtain an integer solution from a linear programming solution. The results of the study show that the proposed algorithm is effective, and the results of the simulation demonstrate that the data transfer time is significantly impacted by the allocation of the processing units.

A novel simulation model has been developed to accurately replicate the dynamics of monopods traversing soft, deformable terrains. This model is based on a combination of physical principles and mathematical equations that account for the monopod's interaction with the ground. By considering factors such as the monopod's leg penetration depth and the ground's reaction forces, the proposed simulation accurately predicts the monopod's behavior under various hopping conditions. To validate the proposed model, extensive numerical experiments were conducted, demonstrating its ability to accurately model monopod dynamics in both elastic and plastic terrains. Furthermore, the proposed model was applied to optimize monopod design and control parameters, resulting in improved performance and increased monopod longevity.

The widespread deployment of IoT devices in large-scale networks necessitates regular updates to ensure security and functionality. However, the confined storage space on IoT devices poses a significant challenge to updating them efficiently. To address this issue, researchers have proposed an over-the-air update approach using the Lightweight M2M protocol, which allows for updates to be initiated remotely and downloaded in segments. To evaluate the feasibility of this method, a large-scale experiment was conducted on 1000 LoRaWAN nodes, which demonstrated that it is possible to update devices with 100KB of data using 1000 nodes, with an average update time of 10 seconds per device. This breakthrough paves the way for scalable and efficient firmware updates on IoT devices with limited storage space.

We've discovered that the transition point of many-body localization, marked by a change in the system's behavior, can be identified through a specific pattern in its complex energy distribution. This pattern is consistent across different types of interactions and applies to a certain class of systems. Our research also shows that this pattern is connected to another property of the system, known as multifractality, and that both can be understood through a theoretical model.

In our study, we investigate a theoretical model of an agent's search for multiple targets within a limited timeframe, constrained by a set resources. The agent's search process is subject to costs, and she can only make a single purchase per query, constrained by her overall spending limit. The goal of our model is to determine the most efficient strategy for the agent to maximize the probability of finding at least one target within the given resources. The model's solution is expressed in terms of the relative prices of the queries and the probabilities of each target appearing within a query. The model's results are further validated by a proof showing that an optimal strategy exists, and that this strategy is characterized by a specific type of function. The model's implications are also discussed in the context of advertising and search engine design.

Machine learning's vulnerability to adversarial attacks is a well-documented issue, with researchers exploring various defense mechanisms. A recent study delves into the potential for universal adversarial attacks on both classical and quantum machine learning models. By employing a gradient-based approach, the study demonstrates that a single, pre-computed perturbation can achieve high attack success rates across a diverse range of quantum and classical classifiers, including those used for MNIST and FASHION MNIST datasets. Furthermore, the study's results indicate that universal attacks are also effective in identifying misclassified data points without requiring a training process. A comparative analysis of the study's findings with existing approaches reveals that universal attacks offer a more efficient and effective solution, with lower computational costs and higher attack success rates.
We demonstrate that Steklov eigenvalues of nearly circular domains can be accurately approximated using Titchmarsh's expansion, which implies the eigenvalues have Weyl asymptotics.

Trace conformance verification is a crucial process in business process management, ensuring that observed activity sequences adhere to predefined process models. Traditional conformance checking methods, however, struggle with incomplete sequences and are limited in their ability to analyze partial process executions. To address this gap, we propose an innovative approach that validates and aligns incomplete execution paths with reference models, taking into account their inherent structural constraints. By leveraging a novel trace fragment alignment method, we can identify the most suitable alignment between observed paths and reference models, thereby enhancing process compliance and process improvement.

Radio signal propagation in complex urban environments is a highly nonlinear process, which is typically approximated by a computationally intensive Monte Carlo ray-tracing method. This approximation is necessary due to the lack of a precise analytical solution. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of using deep convolutional neural networks to create a more accurate and efficient model for predicting radio signal properties. Our results indicate that deep learning models can achieve a high level of accuracy in replicating the outcomes of Monte Carlo simulations, while being significantly faster and simpler to implement.

This study introduces a comprehensive semantics for temporal planning, focusing on the fundamental concepts of states, actions, and transitions. Our approach ensures that all basic temporal planning constructs are formally defined and that their interactions are explicitly specified. To facilitate this, we propose a formal semantics that can be applied to both discrete-time and continuous time frameworks. Our method also includes the formal verification of temporal planning models using a transition system-based approach, which enables the detection of potential errors in model design. The advantage of our approach lies in its modularity, allowing for the separate development and testing of new temporal constructs without the need for re-verification of existing components.

The responsiveness of power system models to changes in their input parameters is a crucial aspect to consider when making policy decisions. This study examines the responsiveness of power system models, specifically those that account for the integration of renewable energy sources, to variations in key parameters such as investment costs and capacity factors. By analyzing the cost-benefit trade-offs associated with these models, the research aims to provide insights into the robustness of power system expansion plans under different scenarios.
We establish the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and Vlasov-Schrödinger systems within bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$, utilizing the method of energy estimates.

In software engineering, concept location is the process of pinpointing a specific concept within a large codebase. This task is typically performed using keyword search, but determining the optimal keywords to use is a complex challenge. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called STRICT, which utilizes search engines to identify relevant keywords based on the surrounding code context. By leveraging code context, STRICT effectively enhances keyword selection and, as a result, improves the accuracy of concept location. Our experimental findings demonstrate that STRICT outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, with an average F1-score improvement of 10.8% and 11.4% for Java and C/C++ codebases respectively.

The characteristics of a colloidal gel's flow and its structural properties can be modified by adjusting its response to sound waves. This adjustment is achieved by altering the gel's density and the size of its internal structures, which in turn affects the gel's strength and its ability to flow. As a result, gels that initially exhibit a tendency to flow can be transformed into more rigid solids, and the gel's response to stress can be changed from stable to unstable. This phenomenon is observed in a suspension of silica particles and is influenced by the presence of a specific type of molecule that causes the particles to repel each other.

The Collatz Conjecture poses a straightforward yet unresolved mathematical problem. It involves a function f that takes positive integers as input and applies the following rules: if the input is even, divide it by two; if it's odd, multiply it by three and add one. The conjecture asserts that starting with any positive integer n, repeatedly applying this function will always result in one. This article provides an in-depth analysis of the conjecture, including its historical context, underlying logic, associated challenges, and potential connections to broader mathematical theories.

This research aims to refine the classification of document types in the Digital Mathematics Library, a collection of over 1.2 million mathematical papers, by employing a machine learning approach that utilizes mathematical entities to aid in document categorization. Our study compares the efficacy of two classification models, a linear model and a neural network, and evaluates the impact of incorporating mathematical entities on the accuracy of document type predictions. Our findings indicate that neural networks outperform linear models, and that incorporating mathematical entities enhances the accuracy of document type predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of using mathematical entities to aid in the classification of previously unlabelled papers.

In the context of stable matching, we examine how to choose which proposals to make when the size of the proposal set is limited. The goal is to maximize the number of high-priority matches through a specific strategy. We have developed an algorithm that achieves this goal with the highest possible guarantee, at the best time complexity, and in the most efficient priority queue usage. Additionally, we have found that, in some cases, achieving the best outcome requires making the largest possible number of proposals.

To evaluate the quality of summarization models, several automatic assessment metrics have been developed. These include traditional metrics like ROUGE, which compare reference summaries to generated ones, and more recent metrics like SUMScore, which use pre-trained language models to evaluate summaries. However, existing metrics have limitations, such as being unable to assess the diversity of generated summaries or requiring extensive training. To address these issues, we introduce a new assessment metric called Cross-Encoder SUMScore, which uses a pre-trained cross-encoder model to evaluate summaries without the need for additional training. This model outperforms existing metrics on multiple datasets, including Abstractive Summarization and Abstractive Summarization datasets.

We investigate the problem of recovering a sparse signal using an incoherent measurement method that employs a nonlinear transformation. The linear measurements are augmented with the square of each linear measurement. The proposed method is based on the l1-regularized least squares approach, which is shown to yield satisfactory results under a more relaxed condition than traditional compressed sensing techniques. The success of this method is attributed to the low l4-norm of sparse signals, which is shown to be a key factor in achieving sparsity-promoting recovery. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed measurement model can effectively recover sparse signals, with the l4-norm playing a crucial role in this process. The proposed method is shown to be computationally efficient, with the number of measurements required being significantly lower than that required by traditional compressed sensing techniques. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical simulations, which show that the proposed method can effectively recover sparse signals, with the number of measurements required being significantly lower than that required by traditional compressed sensing techniques.

The incorporation of multi-sensory fusion techniques has become a key factor in improving the accuracy of autonomous driving systems. In this research, we introduce a novel method for fusing LiDAR and camera data by combining features derived from both Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) space and image space. The fusion process leverages BEV features from LiDAR data and projects them into image space, where they are combined with camera features. The resulting fused features are then used to enhance the detection capabilities of autonomous vehicles. Our approach, dubbed BEVFusion, demonstrates superior performance on the nuScence dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results with a significant improvement in detection metrics. The code for this method is available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI.github.io/tree/master/Release Autonomous-Driving/BEVFusion.

This research investigates the impact of dissipation-range turbulence in fluids.
We introduce a theoretical model of a turbulence model that is in a state of
constant equilibrium with enhanced dissipation. We demonstrate that the
dissipation rate is significantly higher than expected in classical
turbulence. We also show that the distribution of turbulent kinetic energy is
non-uniform and that small-scale structures are more intense than their large-
scale counterparts.

The formation of periodic structures in a liquid due to localized heating from a laser is investigated through both experimental and computational methods. A model describing the liquid's temperature distribution is developed, which is based on the liquid's thermal properties and laser intensity. This model is then used to calculate the refractive index variations, which are found to be in good agreement with the observed diffraction patterns. A key factor in the model is the liquid's response time to the laser, which is found to be in the range of 10-100 nanoseconds. This model provides a framework for understanding and predicting the formation of periodic structures in response to localized heating in liquids.

To effectively apply machine learning to extract design discussions, it's crucial to establish a stable framework for defining the extraction task. In this study, we examine various methods of framing design discussions, including those used in the Open Design Association's Design Discussion Policy and the GitHub Design Discussion Label, and compare them to a novel approach, the Github Discussion Discussion, which we developed. By analyzing the stability of these frameworks, we aim to provide a standardized method for defining design discussions that can be reliably applied to extraction tasks.

The growing importance of continuous data streams in business processes has led to a need for real-time analytics that can be applied to these streams. However, current data stream processing systems are not designed to handle large volumes of streaming data, making it difficult to perform real-time analytics. In this paper, we propose a new approach to processing data streams that enables real-time analytics by exploiting the benefits of distributed computing and data processing techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by using it to analyze a large dataset of Twitter data, and we show that it can be applied to a variety of data streams and data histories.

This research introduces a novel approach to managing knowledge base elements in neural machine translation, specifically for translating to and from question answering datasets that utilize external knowledge bases. Current methods often struggle with maintaining consistency in translating these elements due to their vast and diverse nature. To address this challenge, we developed a system that utilizes a target language vocabulary to facilitate consistent translations. By incorporating this system, we were able to achieve a 2.5-point improvement in BLEU score on the K270 dataset, bringing our results in line with state-of-the-art approaches.

The reputation of researchers is often evaluated using metrics tied to their citation impact, but these measures can be inaccurate, particularly for researchers whose work is published in fields with low citation rates or in fields that are still developing. An alternative method called venue analytics has been developed to address this issue. This new method assesses the reputation of research groups based on the reputation of the research venues they publish in, rather than individual papers. Our research demonstrates that venue analytics can serve as a reliable indicator of a researcher's traditional citation impact and provides a more accurate evaluation in fields with lower citation rates. Furthermore, we found that using venue analytics can lead to fairer comparisons between researchers and more equitable resource allocation.

This comprehensive review explores the integration of neural networks in control systems, focusing on validation methodologies. The underlying issue of ensuring the safety and reliability of these systems is examined, particularly in the context of increasing applications in safety-critical domains. The review delves into the theoretical aspects of neural networks, their historical development, and current validation techniques, while also considering practical implementation challenges. The discussion is further expanded to encompass reinforcement learning and its role in control, highlighting the need for a thorough understanding of the subject matter to address the challenges associated with deploying neural networks in control systems.

In many practical situations, data points are often connected through multiple relationships, which can be represented as overlapping groups. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel clustering method called FHCO, which incorporates the concept of functorial overlaps to handle such data. Our approach is based on a category that accommodates overlapping sets and a functorial grouping mechanism that can be applied to any data set. By utilizing a minimum spanning tree, we can efficiently compute the overlap functorial grouping for any given data set. Our method is demonstrated through several examples, including a clustering of proteins based on their structural and functional similarities, and a clustering of news articles based on their semantic and temporal relationships.

Tensor loop completion techniques have been widely used in tensor completion tasks, but they have not been extensively applied to image recovery. In this study, we propose a novel approach called PTLc, a streaming tensor loop completion method designed for efficient visual data recovery. PTLc leverages a tensor loop completion framework to iteratively refine and reconstruct visual data. To achieve this, PTLc employs a multi-scale tensor loop completion strategy that incorporates a hierarchical tensor structure, allowing it to capture and model complex visual patterns. By leveraging the tensor loop completion framework, PTLc can accurately reconstruct visual data from limited observations. To further enhance its performance, PTLc incorporates a patch tracking mechanism that dynamically adjusts the tensor loop completion iterations based on the observed visual data. This allows PTLc to adaptively handle varying levels of visual complexity and improve its overall image recovery accuracy. To validate the effectiveness of PTLc, we conducted extensive experiments on real-world visual data and compared its performance against state-of-the-art tensor loop completion methods. The results demonstrate that PTLc outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, making it a promising solution for efficient visual data recovery.

We demonstrate that every Weyl group belongs to an orbit closure of the standard Weyl group under the action of $Z_2 \times Z_2$ and extend our study of Weyl group actions on the Nichols algebra of a braided vector space, specifically focusing on its orbit under a Weyl group that preserves the quadratic relations of the preimage of the Nichols algebra under the canonical surjection.

This research presents fresh findings on the characteristics of the energy spectrum in the regime of turbulent wave turbulence. Through direct numerical simulations of two-dimensional weakly nonlinear waves governed by the Helmholtz-Kirchhoff equation, the energy spectrum was found to follow a specific pattern known as the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum. This outcome was observed in the absence of any external forcing mechanisms, as the energy spectrum's formation was attributed to the initial conditions of the system. The results obtained from the simulations are in line with previous theoretical predictions and numerical studies, further confirming the emergence of turbulent wave dynamics in the system.

This study introduces an analysis of how graph normalization affects the size of maximum weight independent sets in graphs, revealing that normalizing a graph with at least two connected components and non-zero smallest degrees leads to a significant increase in the size of these sets, sometimes exponentially.

This research investigates the thermodynamic properties of monolayer graphene under a thermal gradient and a magnetic field, with electrically induced changes in its structure. Employing the density functional theory, we've calculated the graphene's electronic energy, specific heat, and Seebeck coefficient, and found that these properties are significantly influenced by the applied magnetic field and electron carrier density. Notably, our findings reveal that the Seebeck coefficient can be amplified by up to 1000 times through the application of a suitable magnetic field, and that the specific heat of graphene can be modulated by adjusting the magnetic field strength.

This paper introduces a novel method for simulating articulated neural networks on virtual characters. By combining a static and dynamic neural network, we can accurately model the realistic movement of neural structures in response to character motion. The static network processes input data to determine the shape of the neural structure, while the dynamic network uses motion data to simulate the movement of the neural structure, taking into account factors such as gravity and orientation. By combining these two networks, we can create a realistic and responsive neural system that accurately reflects the movement of neural structures in virtual avatars.

The effectiveness of data augmentation in deep learning models is well-established, particularly in the context of adversarial attacks and defenses. However, the impact of image transformations on human perception has received less attention. A recent study aimed to bridge this gap by investigating how humans respond to severe image transformations. In a controlled experiment, 30 participants were asked to identify objects in distorted images, with the distortions applied using a deep learning augmentation technique. The results showed that humans are significantly more sensitive to these transformations than state-of-the-art image classification models, particularly in the case of high levels of distortion. This finding has significant implications for the development of robust image classification models and the design of effective adversarial attacks and defenses.

We examine the connection between the Askey-Wilson matrix and the quantum group U_q(sl_2). Our analysis involves the action of the Chern-Simons theory on the manifold formed by the product of a 2-sphere and a closed oriented link, where the link's components have charges corresponding to the Askey-Wilson matrix's indices. The partition function's evaluation for this setup yields a q-deformation of the Gauss link invariant, which in turn recovers the Askey-Wilson matrix up to a linear transformation.

We conducted a thorough study of the thermodynamic properties of a 2D cluster with free trimers using quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis focused on the role of exchange coupling strength and temperature, specifically in relation to specific heat and magnetic susceptibility. We discovered that the exchange coupling strength significantly impacts these properties, with the system exhibiting a temperature scaling that changes from power law to universal in the high-temperature regime. Notably, the exchange coupling strength also influences the system's magnetic susceptibility, with the system exhibiting a temperature scaling that changes from power law to universal in the high-temperature regime. Our results suggest that the system's behavior can be understood in terms of a balance between the system's internal energy and its entropy.

Pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable success in natural language processing tasks, particularly zero-shot learning. To optimize performance, researchers have explored various methods, such as adjusting the model's output format and refining its internal representations. This study focuses on a new approach that leverages meta-tuning on specific task datasets to enhance performance. By capitalizing on the inherent structure of each task, this method outperforms previous techniques, achieving a 1.6% improvement in accuracy on the AG News dataset and a 2.4% improvement on the AGQI dataset.
